intro: Many interior designers ask what do interior designers charge per hour because they feel stuck in a cycle of undercharging. The answer varies widely, but relying solely on hourly rates often limits your growth and penalizes your efficiency.
tldr: Hourly billing often traps you in a cycle of working more for less money.
Most successful firms use a hybrid model or flat fees to protect their margins.
Tracking your time accurately for one week is the best way to uncover your true hourly cost.

blocks.text: Why hourly billing hurts your design business

When you bill by the hour, you are essentially selling your time rather than your expertise. If you become faster at drafting in AutoCAD or creating mood boards in Photoshop, you effectively give yourself a pay cut. This model creates a ceiling on your income because there are only so many hours in a week.
The hidden costs of poor pricing strategy

items: Burnout from working 60 plus hours a week without scaling revenue.
Scope creep where you absorb the costs of endless client revisions.
Operational errors caused by managing invoices and procurement in messy spreadsheets.
Lower profit margins that leave no room for business growth or taxes.

blocks.text: How to fix your pricing without new software

Start by auditing your current workflow. Use a simple timer to track exactly how long you spend on specific tasks for one week. You might find that you spend 60 percent of your time on administrative work rather than design. Once you know your true cost of time, you can set flat fees that account for your overhead and expertise.
Always include a clear revision limit in your client agreements. Define exactly what is included in your base fee to prevent scope creep before it starts.

faq.question: Should I publish my hourly rates on my website?
faq.answer: Most designers do not. Only 20 percent of designers publish their fees. Keep your pricing flexible until you understand the scope of the project.

faq.question: How do I stop scope creep?
faq.answer: Use a written contract that specifies the number of revisions included. Charge an additional fee for any work that falls outside the original agreement.
